source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas?
finding: Atypicality (Uzzi A-index) and disruption (D-index) are negatively related across about 41M papers. Atypical work extends ideas into new areas. Disruptive work replaces a dominant idea inside its own topic. The paper also used an LLM as a measuring tool: topic similarity and a theory-vs-method label.
numbers: 41M articles (1965-2020 figures use about 40.9M). Top 5% atypical cut A>22.9; top 5% displacing cut D>0.04. Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct labelled about 50k highly cited D>0 papers as theory or method, zero-shot, using token probabilities. Prompt variants (few-shot, reworded options, extra 'other' option) reported to give the same trend.
quote: A novel combination (like a hypothetical 'microwave TV') may be creative, but it is unlikely to replace either
limits: Correlational preprint. LLM labels not checked against human labels in the text read.
agent_relevance: Two kinds of attempt exist: distant combination (cross-topic) and displacement (replace the main idea in-topic). They need separate operators and separate checks, not one 'be novel' instruction.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert review: ideas from an LLM agent were rated more novel than expert human ideas, and slightly weaker on feasibility. A human rerank of the AI ideas raised novelty a little more.
numbers: Novelty mean on 1-10: human 4.84 (n=119 reviews), AI 5.64 (n=109), AI plus human rerank 5.81 (n=109). Both AI arms differ from human at p<0.05. 49 ideas per condition, 79 reviewers, 7 NLP topics.
limits: Novelty is judged by people, not computed from a combination metric. NLP prompting topics only. Reviewer agreement only 56.1%. Follow-up (c03) shows the edge does not survive execution.
agent_relevance: Generate many, then rank, can raise perceived novelty. Do not treat perceived novelty as proof of value.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: 43 experts each spent 100+ hours executing randomly assigned LLM or human ideas. After execution LLM ideas lost far more score than human ideas on all four metrics; rankings flipped on many metrics.
numbers: Change after execution (1-10): human novelty -0.010, excitement +0.078, effectiveness -0.052; AI novelty -1.049, excitement -1.760, effectiveness -1.879 (larger drop for AI, p<0.05). After execution AI vs human: excitement 3.90 vs 4.48, effectiveness 4.13 vs 4.78 (flip not significant, N=43). Ideation score vs execution score correlation weak; moderately negative for AI excitement.
limits: N=43 projects, NLP only, one idea generator.
agent_relevance: Novelty seen at the idea stage predicts outcome weakly. The agent should test an unusual attempt cheaply before ranking it above a conventional one.

source: Si et al. (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? (diversity and self-evaluation results)
finding: Plain over-generation stops giving new ideas because duplicates pile up. LLM judges barely beat chance at ranking ideas the way experts do.
numbers: Of 4000 seed ideas per topic only about 200 (about 5%) are non-duplicates at cosine similarity 0.8 (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). Best LLM ranker (Claude-3.5 pairwise) accuracy 53.3% vs human-human consistency 56.1%; GPT-4o direct 50.0%, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0%, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7%, AI Scientist reviewer 43.3%.
limits: Duplicate test is an embedding threshold; a different threshold changes the count.
agent_relevance: Sampling more from one prompt hits a diversity ceiling. Forced distance (different seeds, different fields) is needed to reach atypical regions. Do not let the same model grade its own novelty.

source: Gupta, Pruthi (2025) All That Glitters is Not Novel: Plagiarism in AI Generated Research
finding: Experts told to look for overlap found that many LLM-generated research proposals copy existing work in disguise. Automated plagiarism checks missed it.
numbers: 13 experts, 50 documents (36 proposals from the Si et al. pipeline plus 14 showcased exemplars). 14.0% scored 5 (direct copy, one-to-one method map) and 10.0% scored 4, so 24% verified plagiarism; the other 76% showed partial overlap and only a small fraction looked fully novel. Source-paper authors cross-verified.
limits: Mostly NLP proposals from one pipeline. Each expert scored 3 of 5 proposals.
agent_relevance: A novelty check that embeds the idea and looks for near neighbours can pass a paraphrase. The agent's novelty test needs a method-level mapping (steps and mechanism), not text similarity.

source: Schopf, Farber (2026) Is this Idea Novel? An Automated Benchmark for Judgment of Research Ideas (RINoBench)
finding: LLMs write novelty reasoning that matches human experts, but their final novelty score is poor and avoids the extremes.
numbers: 1,381 expert-judged ideas. Best macro-F1 only 17.2 (GPT-5); o3 16.2. F1 for class 1 (not novel) was 0.0 for every model. Predictions concentrate on classes 3 and 4. MAE about 1 on a 5-point scale. Reasoning models only slightly better than non-reasoning.
limits: Gold labels are expert ratings; five-class scale is hard even for humans.
agent_relevance: Never use a single self-rated novelty number as a gate. The model will say 'moderately novel' for everything. Use pairwise or retrieval-grounded checks.

source: Schopf, Schreieder, Aizawa (2026) Think-Probe-Respond: Improving LLMs as Judges of Research Idea Novelty
finding: Six frontier LLMs show a medium-novelty bias. Probing the model's hidden state mid-reasoning and conditioning the answer on that probe reduced the bias.
numbers: Baseline macro-F1: Gemini 2.5 Pro 15.6, Gemini 3 Pro 15.3, Claude Sonnet 4.5 15.5, Claude Opus 4.5 17.1, GPT-5 mini 16.2, GPT-5.4 15.1. TPR gives +22.30% on average over strong baselines on open models (Qwen3 4B/14B/32B, Gemma-3, Llama-3.1, GPT-OSS-20B).
limits: Needs hidden-state access, so it cannot run through a closed API. Gains are relative; absolute F1 stays about 20-25 on a 5-class task.
agent_relevance: The bias sits in the output step, not in understanding. A scaffold can force a comparison against a named reference list before any score is written.

source: Liu, Yang, Poria, Nguyen, Cambria (2025) Harnessing LLMs for Scientific Novelty Detection
finding: Text-similarity retrieval alone is not enough for novelty detection. A retriever trained on LLM idea summaries, followed by an LLM cross-check, beat earlier baselines.
numbers: Two new datasets (marketing, NLP). Improvement over best baseline: marketing accuracy/precision/recall/F1 +24.11/+25.46/+24.11/+26.69%; NLP +22.54/+28.29/+22.54/+22.82%. NLP accuracy 0.7474 for the full method vs 0.61 for vanilla RAG.
limits: Binary novel / not novel on reference-closure sets; small domain set; preprint.
agent_relevance: Retrieve by idea (purpose and mechanism), not by words, before judging novelty.

source: Radensky, Shahid, Fok, Siangliulue, Hope, Weld (2026) Scideator
finding: A human-LLM system recombines purpose, mechanism and evaluation facets from papers, with distance-controlled retrieval (same topic to entirely different areas). It gave more creativity support than the same LLM without facets.
numbers: Creativity Support Index median 70.5 (Q1 57.5, Q3 79.0) vs baseline 61.0 (Q1 42.25, Q3 71.5), Wilcoxon p<.01; gains in exploration and expressiveness. Novelty checker did not raise confidence overall (sign test n.s., 17 participants), but users revised most when it said 'not novel'. Zero-shot classifier accuracy 0.68, macro-F1 0.65 vs AI Scientist prompt 0.47 and 0.44.
limits: Computer-science researchers; small user study. Four facet pairs at each of three distance levels per run; the distance labels were checked only in a small annotation study.
agent_relevance: A template for an operator that picks a source at a chosen distance and swaps one facet when an idea is 'not novel'. A 'not novel' verdict can be checked against papers; a 'novel' verdict cannot.

source: Wang, Downey, Ji, Hope (2024) SciMON: Scientific Inspiration Machines Optimized for Novelty
finding: Retrieve inspirations from past papers, then loop: compare the idea with its nearest prior ideas and tell the model to be less similar. GPT-4 alone gave ideas with low technical depth and low novelty.
numbers: k=20 nearest neighbours by SentenceBERT. First novelty iteration: 88.9% of updated ideas substantially different from the first draft, 55.6% judged more novel. Six NLP expert raters, 50 instances. GPT-4 few-shot beat zero-shot in 65% of pairs.
limits: Small human studies. 'Novel' means lower similarity to a training-set corpus, which can reward odd rather than good ideas.
agent_relevance: A retrieve-compare-revise loop is a working novelty operator. Pair it with a value check so it does not merely move away from the nearest neighbour.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Nova: An Iterative Planning and Search Approach to Enhance Novelty and Diversity of LLM Generated Ideas
finding: Planned multi-step retrieval of outside knowledge gives more unique novel ideas than one-shot retrieval or no retrieval.
numbers: 3.4x more unique novel ideas than baseline; at least 2.5x more top-rated ideas (Swiss tournament, 170 seed papers); 619 ideas at score 4 and 2521 at score 5. Ablation: without planning unique ideas stay flat (42.4 at step 2, 44.1 at step 3); without planning and retrieval 25.3, 30.6, 31.35.
limits: Novelty judged by LLM plus embedding threshold (cosine 0.3) against top-10 retrieved papers; ranking by Claude-3.5 pairwise, which c04 shows is near chance against experts.
agent_relevance: Fresh outside input each round keeps novelty rising. Repeating the same retrieval stalls.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) Deep Ideation: designing LLM agents to generate novel research ideas on a scientific concept network
finding: Explore-expand-evolve over a keyword network, with an idea stack and a critic trained on reviewer feedback, improved idea quality.
numbers: Average score +10.67% over the best baseline across four AI domains (DL 10.92%, NLP 9.48%, CV 13.91%).
limits: Quality scored by their own critic and LLM judges; human evaluation is small. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A stack of earlier attempts and their scores is a usable memory for choosing the next combination.

source: Gu et al. (2025) LLMs can realize combinatorial creativity
finding: Retrieving across abstraction levels, then recombining structured parts (problem structure, mechanism, principle), gave ideas closer to what the real papers did.
numbers: 87 OAG-Bench papers, 3-5 key references each, Claude-3.5-Sonnet. SPECTER cosine similarity to the real paper up 7-10% over direct generation; key-mechanism similarity about 0.85-0.95 vs 0.7-0.8.
limits: Measures closeness to published work, not novelty. Preprint, single backbone.
agent_relevance: Abstracting a source to a principle before transfer makes distant combinations usable. Score outcome fit, not only novelty.

source: Chen, Zhang (2026) Enhancing research idea generation through combinatorial innovation and multi-agent iterative search
finding: Multi-agent iterative planning with knowledge search raised diversity, novelty and high-score ratio over NOVA and AI-Researcher; generated ideas rated between accepted and rejected ICLR 2025 papers.
numbers: Diversity 0.898 vs NOVA 0.867 vs AI-Researcher 0.680. Novelty 0.133 vs 0.107 vs 0.067. High-score ratio 0.184 vs 0.026 vs 0.013. Comparison set ICLR 2025: 842 accepted and 803 rejected NLP papers.
limits: Same LLM-based metrics as c11. Absolute novelty values are small. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Even the best loops sit between accepted and rejected human work. Expect no free novelty.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Structuring Scientific Innovation: modeling and discovering impactful knowledge combinations
finding: A contrastive model learns what past disruptive problem-method pairs look like; an LLM chain-of-thought Monte Carlo search proposes method combinations scored by a disruption index.
numbers: Reported to beat state-of-the-art on predicting disruptiveness of problem-method pairs. Exact figures not extracted.
limits: The target is a citation-based disruption score, which c23-c25 criticise. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A search loop whose objective is disruption rather than atypicality. The two scores are different targets.

source: Wang (2024) A content-based novelty measure for scholarly publications: a proof of concept
finding: Novelty as atypical word sequences: average surprisal under a language model of scholarly text. Papers experts called novel had higher surprisal.
numbers: 83 working notes, 3 experts, binary novelty. One-tailed Welch t=2.6, p=0.005, df about 66.3 (GPT-2 trained only on English Wikipedia). 8 false alarms with surprisal above 5.0 (maths notation, non-standard syntax).
limits: Proof of concept, small N, one task. Surprisal also rises for odd formatting and equations.
agent_relevance: A cheap token-level atypicality signal exists inside any LM. It confuses odd style with odd ideas.

source: Wu, Zhang, Zhao (2025) Automated novelty evaluation of academic paper: human expertise plus LLMs
finding: The authors doubt that unique reference combinations (Uzzi style) measure novelty. A model tuned on review sentences about novelty plus an LLM summary of the method section predicts method novelty better than prompted LLMs.
numbers: SciBERT accuracy 0.74, F1 0.73 with review and LLM-summary inputs. The tuned model beat prompted LLMs including GPT-4o; Llama 3.1 was the only LLM that gained when human and LLM knowledge were added.
limits: Labels come from peer-review comments on method novelty; method novelty only. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Novelty judgments improve when given human-written reasons. Keep a bank of reviewer-style 'why this is not new' notes.

source: Huang (2026) Catalyst papers in AI research: a landscape on ICLR 2017-2025
finding: Four disruptiveness measures disagree. A zero-shot gpt-4o-mini rater of title and abstract did worse than chance at spotting highly cited papers. Review scores did not predict later disruption.
numbers: 36,113 ICLR papers. AUC for top 2% cited (n=739): EDM 0.83, CD index 0.60, node2vec 0.49, LLM rater 0.42. Rater vs citation velocity rho +0.016 (ns); EDM +0.300; CD +0.127. Review score vs EDM rho about 0.005; accepted vs rejected EDM p=0.11. Topic initiators precede 7.55x topic-share growth; topic bridges precede 11.52x cross-topic citation flow. Five LLMs from four vendors agreed closely with each other.
limits: One venue. LLM rater used one prompt, no ablation. The second label set came from another LLM (9 positives).
agent_relevance: Agreement across vendors is not validity. A model that agrees with other models can still miss what later matters. The bridge vs initiator split echoes atypical vs disruptive.

source: Yan, Ni (2026) AI-assisted writing and the reorganization of scientific knowledge
finding: After 2023, papers with more AI-assisted text are more disruptive (CD index) within the same author and field, yet their cross-field citation breadth does not grow. More displacement from narrower inputs.
numbers: About 2M full-text articles 2021-2024. 18-month window beta=0.151 (SE 0.004, p<0.001); 12m 0.152; 24m 0.171. Yearly effect 2022 -0.116, 2023-24 +0.321 to +0.408. Breadth (entropy) effect fell from 1.277 (2021) and 1.225 (2022) to 0.455 (2024); concentration (HHI) effect from -0.561/-0.539 to -0.207.
limits: Observational. AI use is a text-detector estimate, not observed. Mostly PubMed Central, biomedical. Could be style change.
agent_relevance: Machine-assisted work can look disruptive without drawing on more distant sources. Supports tracking the two axes separately.

source: Safari, Babaei (2026) Research novelty in Information Systems journals after ChatGPT
finding: Semantic novelty fell more after 2022 for first authors from non-English-dominant countries than for English-dominant ones.
numbers: 13,847 articles 2020-2025, 44 A*/A IS journals, SPECTER2 distance to nearest recent papers. Post x Non-EDA -0.176 SD (p<0.001), about 7 percentile points; -0.157 with journal fixed effects. Pre-trend 2020: 0.003 (p=0.914).
limits: Individual LLM use not observed; authors say the result is not an effect of LLM adoption. Embedding novelty reflects how a paper is presented.
agent_relevance: Embedding-distance novelty moves with language and framing, so it is a noisy gate for the agent's own output.

source: Wenger, Kenett (2025) We're Different, We're the Same: Creative Homogeneity Across LLMs
finding: 22 LLMs were about as original as humans on average but far more alike each other than humans are to each other. A creativity system prompt helped only slightly.
numbers: Originality means (LLM vs human): AUT 0.711 vs 0.696, FF 0.603 vs 0.637, DAT 0.801 vs 0.753. Population variability (cosine distance between embedded answers) significantly lower for LLMs on all three tests. LLM answers share more words, which explains part of it.
limits: Short tests (object uses, word lists), not research ideas.
agent_relevance: Switching to another model does not give a different region. For distant combinations vary the source material or the operator, not the model.

source: Doshi, Hauser (2024) Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
finding: Access to AI ideas improved individual story ratings but made the set of stories more alike. Not opened this session; taken from a search summary.
numbers: Reported 10.7% lower collective diversity (search summary only, not checked in the source).
limits: Publisher page returned 403. Treat the number as unverified.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as c21 at the group level.

source: Larregue, Gingras (2026) The disruption index does not measure scientific innovation
finding: A sociology critique: the disruption index is a black-boxed measure taken on common-sense intuition and may not match the concept of disruption. It comments on a Science policy article linking disruption to academic age.
numbers: No new tests; argument about construct validity.
limits: Opinion piece; limited data.
agent_relevance: Do not use a CD-type score as the agent's goal. Use it only as a descriptive signal.

source: Holst, Algaba, Tori, Wenmackers, Ginis (2024) Dataset artefacts are the hidden drivers of the declining disruptiveness in science
finding: Failed replication of the decline-in-disruption claim: the decline comes from database entries with zero references, which have CD index of 1. Even random citing reproduces the decline.
numbers: Park et al. used about 45M papers and 3.9M patents. The reanalysis says the decline follows a relative fall of zero-reference entries and that the original robustness checks missed it.
limits: Reanalysis of one data set; others (c26) dispute other parts of the disruption story.
agent_relevance: The headline that science is becoming less disruptive is not a safe premise for tuning an agent.

source: Huang, Xie (2026) Large scientific teams are more, not less, disruptive
finding: The reported small-team disruption advantage is largely a measurement artifact: the standard disruption index falls mechanically as reference lists lengthen.
numbers: About 60M publications. Equalizing reference counts reverses the gradient. A one-reference-at-a-time measure separates breakthroughs better across six benchmarks including the Nobel Prize. Disruption rises with team size in four domains and every decade 1970s-2010s.
limits: Authors' new measure is itself new and not independently validated.
agent_relevance: Disruption results flip with specification. The agent should not copy human-science rules (small, focused, etc.) taken from this metric.

source: Wei et al. (2026) Identifying disruptive models in the open-source LLM community
finding: A Model Disruption Index on Hugging Face lineage shows most open models are consolidating, not disruptive. The disruption idea is applied to AI systems themselves.
numbers: 2,556,240 models. Most consolidative; disruptive positions more likely among large models and through fine-tuning.
limits: Lineage tags are self-reported on the Hub; no ablation of the index.
agent_relevance: Same 'mostly consolidating' pattern as human science; a sign that a default loop will mostly refine.
